I could only read three sources: David Guzik's Enduring Word commentary (the full page I fetched ends at v. 18; I have only the search-result summary for vv. 21 and 25–26), the Pulpit Commentary on Bible Hub (the full page ends at v. 19; vv. 21, 24 and 26 come from the search excerpt), and an excerpt from Precept Austin. The research tools stopped working before I could open Ellicott, Gill, the tradition-specific sites, Bible Odyssey, the NET Bible notes, or the Catholic and Orthodox sites. So sections 2 and 3 have nothing yet, and v. 22 has no notes.

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** Guzik says Jesus's burial was done in a hurry, so the women came to finish it properly. He cites Liefeld: the first day became the Christian day of worship, and moving away from the Sabbath is itself strong evidence for the Resurrection. He also cites Trapp: by God's providence the women arrived before the apostles, which answers the priests' story that the disciples stole the body. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-24/
- The Pulpit Commentary follows Westcott in suggesting two separate groups of women came to the tomb. Luke tells of the second group, which included Joanna. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/24.htm

**v. 2:** Guzik: the stone wasn't moved to let Jesus out, since His risen body could pass through barriers. It was moved so others could see inside and be convinced. He also says the stone answers the swoon theory and the theory that animals took the body. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-24/
- The Pulpit Commentary describes rock-cut tombs of the time and points to early witnesses to the traditional site: the Bordeaux Pilgrim (AD 333), Cyril of Jerusalem and Eusebius. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/24.htm

**v. 3:** Guzik notes that none of the Gospels describes the Resurrection itself, only its discovery. Quoting Pate, he says this plainness supports the accounts' historical truth. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-24/

**v. 4:** Guzik: the women were puzzled, which shows they weren't expecting a resurrection, so the accounts can't be wishful thinking. As angels announced Jesus's birth to humble people, they announce His resurrection to a few women. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-24/
- Pulpit Commentary: one group saw one angel and another saw two, but the message was the same. It quotes Lessing's point that the Gospel writers weren't counting angels. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/24.htm

**v. 5:** Guzik uses Morris (Jesus isn't to be thought of as dead, so He isn't to be looked for among the dead) and Clarke (graves were unclean places where no one would look for the living). His application is that people still look for Jesus in dead things, such as empty ritual, man-made rules and human effort. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-24/

**v. 6:** Guzik: no tomb of Jesus will ever be found, because "He is not here." He also says the women knew exactly which tomb it was (Luke 23:55), which answers the wrong-tomb theory. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-24/
- Pulpit Commentary: "He is not here, but is risen" appears in every angelic message at the tomb. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/24.htm

**v. 7:** Guzik: "must" is the key word. The Resurrection was as necessary and ordained as the cross (compare Luke 18:31–33). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-24/

**v. 8:** Guzik: the empty tomb and the angels couldn't change the women's hearts on their own; it was Jesus's words that brought the first hope. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-24/
- Spurgeon (quoted on Precept Austin): it's good to know Christ's words even if we often forget them, because some will come back to us when we need them. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-24-commentary

**v. 9:** Pulpit Commentary: Luke's tomb scene is the least vivid of the four Gospels. It suggests he got it years later from one of the women. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/24.htm

**v. 10:** Guzik gives background on each woman. Mary Magdalene had seven demons cast out of her. Joanna was the wife of Chuza, Herod's steward, and probably well-off. Mary the mother of James was probably the mother of James the Less. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-24/

**v. 11:** Guzik, citing Barclay, says the word for "nonsense" was a medical term for a fevered person's raving. He quotes Pate (women's testimony wasn't counted as authoritative then, so including it shows Luke's high regard for women) and Morris (the disciples were deeply skeptical). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-24/
- Pulpit Commentary: the disciples didn't expect anything, while the Sanhedrin feared something would happen after three days. The Gospels openly admit the disciples' surprise, which supports their honesty. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/24.htm

**v. 12:** Guzik reads this alongside John 20:3–9. Peter saw the grave clothes lying in order, but he had forgotten Jesus's words, so he wondered rather than believed. Without Jesus's words, Guzik says, the Resurrection doesn't make sense: "the cross was the payment and the empty tomb is the receipt." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-24/
- Pulpit Commentary: some ancient manuscripts leave this verse out, but the commentary says it is "no doubt genuine," a short version of John 20:3–10. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/24.htm

**v. 13:** Guzik: these two weren't famous apostles but ordinary followers, which shows a Saviour for the common man (quoting Morrison). He quotes Pate that Emmaus's location is uncertain, and Plummer that Luke probably got the story from one of the two. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-24/
- Pulpit Commentary: this story is found only in Luke. The name Emmaus may refer to warm springs, and the commentary places it at modern Kulonieh. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/24.htm

**v. 14:** Guzik: they talked about what weighed most on their hearts, Jesus's arrest and crucifixion. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-24/

**v. 15:** Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik): when two believers talk about Christ, He is likely to join them. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-24/
- Pulpit Commentary: an early fulfilment of "where two or three are gathered…" (with Malachi 3:16). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/24.htm

**v. 16:** Pulpit Commentary: some mysterious change had come over the risen Lord. It quotes Westcott: after the Resurrection, Jesus was recognized only when He chose and when the viewer was in spiritual harmony with Him. Grief kept these two from seeing. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/24.htm
- Guzik: they were kept from recognizing Him by a miracle. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-24/

**v. 17:** Pulpit Commentary: older manuscripts end the question at "as you walk along" and then add "they stood still, looking sad," which makes the scene more vivid. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/24.htm

**v. 18:** Pulpit Commentary: the name Cleopas is a Greek short form of Cleopatros and suggests a background in Alexandria. Plumptre thought he might have given Luke this otherwise unknown story. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/24.htm

**v. 19:** Pulpit Commentary: both disciples probably blurted out "Jesus of Nazareth," the name everyone in the city was talking about. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/24.htm

**v. 21:** Guzik: their hope wasn't really disappointed, but it was misdirected. Jesus would show them their true hope was fulfilled in Him. These disciples had a hope disappointed. Their hope was not truly disappointed; but in some ways their hope was misguided (**that it was He who was going to redeem Israel**). Jesus would show them that their true hope was fulfilled in Him and His resurrection. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-24/
- Pulpit Commentary: they understood "redeemer" in a different sense from Christians, yet the idea was still something very lofty and sublime. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/24.htm

**vv. 23–24:** Guzik: Jesus wanted to know if they could believe without seeing. We can believe and must believe based on the reliable eyewitness testimony of other people. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-24/
- Pulpit Commentary quotes Tholuck: their words sound like hearts where "the smoking flax yet glimmers," though nearly out. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/24.htm

**vv. 25–26:** Guzik: They should have believed what **all the prophets have spoken**, that the Messiah would suffer first and then be received in glory. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-24/
- Pulpit Commentary puts Jesus's meaning in its own words: the prophets plainly foretold the Messiah's suffering and death before His triumph, and the disciples had missed it. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/24.htm
